How tidycreel Chooses an Estimator

Source: vignettes/estimator-choice.Rmd
estimator-choice.Rmd

estimate_effort(), estimate_catch_rate() and estimate_total_catch() are each one function, but behind each is more than one estimator. This page explains which one runs, what decides it, and how to see afterwards which one was used.

Two things decide it, both fixed when the design is built:

survey_type    (creel_design)    -> how effort is estimated, and how totals are built
interview_type (add_interviews)  -> how the catch rate is estimated

Neither is chosen by looking at the data. The estimator follows from how the data were collected, which the design records, so the same data attached to the same design always get the same estimator.

library(tidycreel)

The map

survey_type Effort Catch rate Total catch
"instantaneous" counts × period length, summed over the sampled days, or expanded to every day of the stratum with target by interview_type (below) per stratum, effort × rate, summed over strata
"aerial" counts × hours open × angler ratio ÷ visibility by interview_type per stratum, effort × rate, summed over strata
"bus_route" Horvitz-Thompson: each interviewed trip’s effort over its inclusion probability ratio of the Horvitz-Thompson catch and effort totals Horvitz-Thompson catch total
"ice" as bus route, with every site’s p_site = 1 as bus route as bus route
"camera" not estimate_effort(): est_effort_camera() calibrates counts against interview effort by interview_type refused

Sectioned instantaneous designs (add_sections()) estimate each section separately and add a lake total.

Whether the effort covers only the days counted or every day in the season is a separate choice, target, not a different estimator. The default, "sampled_days", is the effort on the days counted; "period_total" expands each stratum to all its days. On the season data used below, that is 3,066 angler-hours against about 9,994. Totals follow the effort they are given, so a catch total on the default target is the catch on the sampled days. vignette("effort-pipeline") explains the expansion, and the expanded targets are not yet available for bus-route or ice designs.

The pages that explain each estimator in full:

  • instantaneous-count effort and its two-stage variance: vignette("effort-pipeline");
  • rates and totals from interviews: vignette("catch-pipeline");
  • bus-route and ice: vignette("bus-route-surveys"), vignette("ice-fishing"), and the equations in vignette("bus-route-equations");
  • aerial: vignette("aerial-surveys"), and the model-based alternative, estimate_effort_aerial_glmm(), in vignette("aerial-glmm");
  • camera: vignette("camera-surveys").

Effort follows the survey type

The survey type says what a count is, and so what turns it into effort.

  • An instantaneous count is the number of anglers present at one moment. Multiplied by the length of the period it was taken in, it estimates that period’s effort. With an expanded target, the sampled days are then expanded to every day of the stratum.
  • An aerial count is an instantaneous count from the air, covering the whole water. It becomes effort through the hours open, the ratio of anglers to people seen, and the share of anglers the observer can see.
  • A bus-route survey does not count anglers at all. The clerk meets every trip that ends at a site while waiting there, and each trip is weighted by the probability that the schedule put the clerk at that site at that time (Jones and Pollock 2012, eq. 19.4). An ice survey is the same design with every site visited whenever its day is sampled (p_site = 1).
  • A camera count is a daily total of arrivals, not a count of anglers present. Summing it over days gives arrivals, not effort. estimate_effort() refuses a camera design for that reason and names est_effort_camera(), which converts counts to effort with a ratio taken from days that have both counts and interviews.

The catch rate follows the interview type

An access interview meets a party as it leaves, so the trip is complete. A roving interview meets a party while it is still fishing. The two sample trips differently, and so they need different estimators (Pollock et al. 1997):

  • Access: the ratio of means, total catch over total effort, on complete trips. Every trip has the same chance of being met whatever its length, so this estimates total catch over total effort, the quantity a total needs.
  • Roving: the mean of the individual catch rates, on all trips. A roving clerk meets a party in proportion to how long it fishes, and under that selection it is the mean of ratios that estimates total catch over total effort (Hoenig et al. 1997). That result is derived for individual anglers, and an interview is a party: meeting a party meets all its anglers. So each party’s rate per angler-hour counts once per angler in it (n_anglers). Without a party size the rate is per party-hour, and each party counts once. Trips shorter than half an hour are left out by default: their rates are mostly noise and inflate the variance.

Why each of these is right, and when, is the subject of vignette("catch-pipeline").

Bus-route and ice designs have their own rate: catch over effort, each a Horvitz-Thompson total. interview_type does not change it.

Totals follow from the two

A total is a rate times an effort, built stratum by stratum and summed, with the standard error from Goodman’s (1960) exact variance of a product. Bus-route and ice totals are different: the catch is weighted by its inclusion probability directly (Jones and Pollock 2012, eq. 19.5), with no product.

Camera designs have no total. Their counts are arrivals, so a rate per angler-hour times a camera count would not be a catch, and estimate_total_catch() refuses rather than report one.

Seeing which estimator ran

Every estimate records how it was made. method names the estimator and, for rates and the totals built from them, estimator names the rate estimator underneath. On the season data, with access and then roving interviews:

design <- creel_design(example_season_calendar, date = date, strata = day_type)
design <- add_counts(design, example_season_counts,
  period_length_col = daylight_hours
)

access <- add_interviews(design, example_season_interviews,
  catch = catch_total, harvest = catch_kept, effort = hours_fished,
  trip_status = trip_status, n_anglers = n_anglers
)
#> ℹ 153 interviews have zero catch.
#>   Zero catch is usual; check it is not missing data recorded as 0.
#> ℹ Added 231 interviews: 172 complete (74%), 59 incomplete (26%)
roving <- add_interviews(design, example_roving_interviews,
  catch = catch_total, harvest = catch_kept, effort = hours_fished,
  trip_status = trip_status, trip_duration = hours_fished,
  n_anglers = n_anglers, interview_type = "roving"
)
#> ℹ 133 interviews have zero catch.
#>   Zero catch is usual; check it is not missing data recorded as 0.
#> ℹ Added 212 interviews: 0 complete (0%), 212 incomplete (100%)

access_rate <- estimate_catch_rate(access)
#> ℹ Using complete trips for CPUE estimation
#>   (n=172, 74.5% of 231 interviews) [default]
roving_rate <- estimate_catch_rate(roving)
#> ℹ Roving design: using all 212 interviews for CPUE via MOR [auto]
#>   (0 complete, 212 incomplete)
#>   Override with `use_trips = 'complete'` for access-point estimation.
#> Warning: ! MOR truncation: 29 trips excluded (13.7%)
#> ℹ Trips < 0.5 hours excluded to prevent unstable variance
#> ! High truncation rate may indicate data quality issues
#> ℹ Consider reviewing trip duration data for errors
#> ℹ Repeats on this design are recorded, not printed: see `get_warnings()`.

c(access = access_rate$method, roving = roving_rate$method)
#>                access                roving 
#> "ratio-of-means-cpue" "mean-of-ratios-cpue"
c(access = access_rate$estimator, roving = roving_rate$estimator)
#>           access           roving 
#> "ratio-of-means"            "mor"

The two messages say the same thing as it happens: complete trips for the access design, and all trips by mean of ratios for the roving one, marked [auto] because the interview type chose it. The roving rate also warns that 29 trips under half an hour were left out. That is expected here: a roving clerk meets many parties early in their trips, and the warning fires whenever 10% or more are removed, so that a data error that shortens trips is noticed.

Overriding the choice

The defaults follow the design, but the rate estimator can be named:

  • estimator: "ratio-of-means", "mor" (mean of ratios), or "mortr" (mean of ratios with trips under truncate_at hours removed);
  • use_trips: "complete" or "all"; the rate functions also take "incomplete", and "diagnostic", which estimates from complete and incomplete trips separately and compares them. A total accepts only "complete" and "all";
  • truncate_at: the shortest trip, in hours, a mean of ratios keeps.

Naming either estimator or use_trips turns off the roving default, so the roving design then gets what was asked for. Some combinations are refused because they are not an estimator: a ratio of means on incomplete trips, which the length bias of incomplete trips makes wrong, and a mean-of-ratios total on a bus-route or ice design, which has no such form.

The variance method (variance = "taylor", "bootstrap" or "jackknife") and the product variance of a total (product_variance = "goodman" or "first_order") are separate choices. They change the standard error, not the estimator; vignette("replicate-designs") and vignette("catch-pipeline") explain them.

References

  • Goodman, L. A. (1960). On the exact variance of products. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 55, 708–713.
  • Hoenig, J. M., Jones, C. M., Pollock, K. H., Robson, D. S., and Wade, D. L. (1997). Calculation of catch rate and total catch in roving surveys of anglers. Biometrics, 53, 306–317.
  • Jones, C. M., and Pollock, K. H. (2012). Recreational angler survey methods: estimation of effort, harvest, and released catch. Chapter 19 in Fisheries Techniques (3rd ed.), pp. 883–919. American Fisheries Society.
  • Pollock, K. H., Hoenig, J. M., Jones, C. M., Robson, D. S., and Greene, C. J. (1997). Catch rate estimation for roving and access point surveys. North American Journal of Fisheries Management, 17, 11–19.
